objectives.text: Keep the 1899 arbitral line and have the ICJ confirm it. Venezuela claims the Essequibo and rejects the 1899 award. Guyana filed at the ICJ on 29 March 2018, and the merits hearings were held 4-11 May 2026; the ICJ page shows no judgment date yet, and Guyana's government expects a ruling as early as November 2026.

objectives.text: Turn the oil windfall into a fund that pays for development at a steady pace. The sovereign wealth fund was set up in 2019 and holds all oil revenue; it lets the government draw money at a steady rate. Reuters calculates Guyana's 2026 oil revenue at about USD 4.3bn at USD 100 a barrel, 67% above last year.

means.text: The ICJ as the legal lever. Guyana takes the border to the court rather than to force. The court indicated provisional measures on 1 December 2023 against changes on the ground and modified its order on 1 May 2025, after Guyana's second request of 6 March 2025.

constraints.text: The operator takes the first oil. An ExxonMobil-led consortium controls all of Guyana's oil production and takes 75% of it to recover costs; profit oil to the state is 12.5% now and is expected to rise to 50% once cost recovery is complete (Exxon has said this could happen in 2026).

constraints.text: The claim is a state policy in Caracas. Venezuela's 2023 referendum (3 December 2023) asked about a Guayana Esequiba state, and a March 2024 law designated the Essequibo as a new Venezuelan state. In May 2026 Venezuela's leader, Delcy Rodriguez, was to defend the claim in person before the court.

paradoxes.text: The oil that pays for the defence of the border is what makes the border worth contesting. Drilling licences granted in September 2023 after the offshore finds triggered the 2023 escalation; the windfall now rising 67% gives Guyana the means to fight the case and gives Venezuela the reason to press it.

grand_strategy.reading: Guyana runs its strategy on three levers: the 1899 line argued at The Hague, oil revenue held in a fund, and an Exxon-led operator that carries the output. Its weakness is that the same oil makes the disputed territory worth claiming, so each step of its growth is also a step in the Venezuelan dispute. Its strength is that a legal case backed by a fund is slow but durable, and the outside partners (Brazil, the United States, the UK, CARICOM, China) are not yet graded because their cards and sources are not written.

stances.note: Guyana toward the claimant to the Essequibo. Mirror of the VEN card's claimed_territory (grievance, stable, since the 1899 award, confidence B), graded one step down as the reciprocal rule requires: from the claimed side a claim against one's own territory reads as rival, not as an open enemy. Guyana holds the territory and takes the dispute to the ICJ, where the merits hearings were held 4-11 May 2026 and the judgment is awaited. Stable because nothing in the 2026 record gives up the claim. Bond grievance: the 1899 award that Venezuela rejects and the 1966 Geneva Agreement. Confidence B on the Venezuelan side only; the Guyanese reading is the mirror of that card, with the same sources. Note for review: the reciprocal rule would give C; the grade is kept at B as instructed for this card.

stances.note: Partner, not ally: the security cooperation is a memorandum and a statement of intent, not a defence treaty (Ali said in the reports read that no treaty had been signed and that the talks would continue). The US is Exxon's home market and the operator's backer: the Exxon-led consortium controls all of Guyana's oil production (Reuters, May 2026), and Reuters notes that US markets are supportive of fossil fuel development. Warming because the security MoU of March 2025 was followed by a Statement of Intent on military cooperation, as reported (date not confirmed). Bond none: pure interest, no kinship or grievance. Confidence C: the grade is our reading of the structure; no source in hand calls the relationship an alliance or a partnership in those words, and the dates of the second instrument are not confirmed.

stances_toward.note: The Essequibo: Venezuela claims the two-thirds of Guyana that the 1899 arbitral award gave to British Guiana, and rejects the award. The claim is what the state says it is for: the ICJ case Guyana brought in 2018 is contested by Caracas, which says the 1966 Geneva Agreement requires direct talks and denies the court competence; the court issued provisional measures in 2023 and May 2025 against changing the situation or holding elections in the region, and one source says Venezuela held them anyway. Judgment expected Nov 2026 to Jan 2027. Stable: nothing in the 2026 record gives up the claim. Bond grievance: the 1899 award and the 1966 agreement. Mirror: Guyana has no card yet, so no Guyanese reading exists; the claim is graded from Caracas alone.
